pages.title: The three-phase induction motor
pages.for: The constant-speed workhorse. Its three windings make a field that turns. The rotor follows a little behind, and that slip makes its torque.
pages.rule:
ns = 120 × f ÷ p
Slip = (ns − n) ÷ ns
Nameplate just under 3000 rpm on 50 Hz: two poles. Just under 1500 rpm: four.

On 50 Hz the field turns at 3000 or 1500 rpm. On 60 Hz, 3600 or 1800 rpm.
Full-load slip is a few percent. More load, more slip, more torque.
Direct on line it draws about 6 to 8 times rated current, sometimes over 10.

traps.text: No slip, no torque. Under its own power the rotor never reaches synchronous speed, because then nothing would sweep past the bars.
To reverse it, isolate, then swap any two of the three line leads.
Single phasing: at rest it hums and will not start. If it is running, the other two lines carry about 173% of their normal current, or more. It overheats fast.
A lightly loaded motor can still draw much of its rated current, at a poor power factor. At light load, current is a poor measure of load.
A good insulation reading cannot prove a motor good. Compare the three winding resistances too. A good winding's readings agree within about 1%.

pages.where: pumps, fans, compressors and conveyors, ashore and at sea.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: Three coils sit 120° apart round a ring. Each carries one phase of a three-phase supply. What does their combined magnetic field do?
pages.answer: It turns round the ring at a steady speed
pages.alt: The three currents peak in turn, a third of a cycle apart. So the strongest point of the field moves from coil to coil, and the field turns.
options: It turns round the ring at a steady speed
It stays put and pulses, stronger then weaker
It turns at whatever speed the rotor turns
pages.html: The three currents peak in turn, a third of a cycle apart. So the strongest point of the field moves from coil to coil, and the field turns.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
Three windings sit 120 electrical degrees apart, one on each phase. Together they make one field that turns at a steady speed, the [[synchronous speed]]: ns = 120 × f ÷ p. On 50 Hz, two poles turn at 3000 rpm and four poles at 1500 rpm.

The field sweeps past the shorted rotor bars and induces a current in them. That current, sitting in the field, pushes the bars round after it.

If the rotor caught the field, nothing would sweep the bars. No current, no torque. So it always runs a little behind. That shortfall, (ns − n) ÷ ns, is the [[slip]].

pages.name: Seen from the rotor
pages.text: On the four-pole motor at full load, the field gains on the rotor by 63 rpm. The slip is 4.2%. The rotor current runs at 2.1 Hz. The torque is 1.00 times rated. With less load, the slip, the rotor current and the torque all shrink. Unloaded, they fall almost to zero, because a real motor still slips a little.
pages.alt: Field slides past the bars: 63 rpm Field Current in a bar Torque At 0% the picture puts the rotor at ns. A real motor never quite gets there. Even unloaded, it slips a little to turn its own bearings and fan. Royal Navy ships run their main supply at 60 Hz. On 60 Hz the field turns a fifth faster than on 50 Hz. At 0% the picture puts the rotor at ns. A real motor never quite gets there. Even unloaded, it slips a little to turn its own bearings and fan.

Royal Navy ships run their main supply at 60 Hz. On 60 Hz the field turns a fifth faster than on 50 Hz.

Slip4.20%(ns − n) ÷ ns
Rotor current frequency2.10 Hzslip × f
Torque1.00 × rated

At full load, the rotor runs 63 rpm behind the field. That slip makes enough current in the bars for the full rated torque.

Load slows the rotor a little. The field then sweeps past the bars faster and induces more voltage in them. More current flows, so the torque rises until it matches the load.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A pump motor runs at full load. Then the pump's load drops away. What happens to the rotor's speed?
pages.answer: It rises towards synchronous speed but stays just below it
pages.alt: Less load needs less torque. Less torque needs less rotor current, and so less slip. The rotor speeds up until its torque matches the load again. It stops short of ns, because at ns there would be no torque at all.
options: It rises towards synchronous speed but stays just below it
It rises until it matches synchronous speed
pages.html: Less load needs less torque. Less torque needs less rotor current, and so less slip. The rotor speeds up until its torque matches the load again. It stops short of ns, because at ns there would be no torque at all.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Speed: Nearly constant. Full-load slip is a few percent, usually under 5%. Just under 3000 rpm on 50 Hz means two poles. Just under 1500 rpm means four.

Starting: Direct on line it draws 6 to 8 times rated current, sometimes over 10. Starting torque varies with the design, so check the data sheet.

Stalling: Load it past its peak torque and it stalls. It then draws starting current and overheats unless its protection trips.

Power factor: Poor at light load. The magnetising current hardly changes with load, so a lightly loaded motor still draws much of its rated current.

A wound rotor brings its winding out on slip rings. Resistance there gives more starting torque, at the cost of brushes to look after.

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Constant-speed work: pumps, fans, compressors and conveyors. At sea it drives these up to 700 kW or more, totally enclosed. The UK chose an induction motor to drive the Type 45 destroyer.

Its limits

A big starting current, which can dip the supply voltage.

Its speed is fixed by the frequency and poles. Changing it needs a variable speed drive.

A poor power factor at light load.

No brushes does not make it safe in a hazardous area. Fit a motor certified for it, to ATEX or IECEx.

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you open the terminal box or the starter.

Single phasing: One line is lost, often through worn starter contacts or a blown fuse. At rest it hums and will not start. Running, the other two lines carry about 173% of normal current. Its protection must trip it.

Wrong rotation: Two lines are swapped somewhere. To reverse it, isolate and swap any two of the three line leads.

Overloads: It runs hot and draws more than rated current until the overload relay trips. Check the relay is set to the nameplate current.

Tests: Insulation resistance finds a wet winding or a short to earth, but cannot prove the motor good. Also compare the three winding resistances. They should agree within about 1%.

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: A pump motor hums and will not start. It was running fine an hour ago. What is the likely cause?
pages.answer: One line is lost: single phasing
pages.alt: With one line gone the field only pulses, so there is no starting torque. A dead fuse, or no current on one line, confirms it. Isolate, then check the fuses and the starter's contacts on each line. Worn contacts are the usual cause.
options: One line is lost: single phasing
Two of the lines have been swapped
pages.html: With one line gone the field only pulses, so there is no starting torque. A dead fuse, or no current on one line, confirms it. Isolate, then check the fuses and the starter's contacts on each line. Worn contacts are the usual cause.
